question: What human foods are toxic to dogs?
answer: The most dangerous, well-documented ones are: xylitol (a sugar substitute), chocolate, grapes and raisins, onions and other allium vegetables, macadamia nuts, alcohol, caffeine, and raw yeast bread dough. Each works by a different mechanism and some are dangerous in tiny amounts (xylitol, grapes), while others depend on dose and size (chocolate, onions). If your dog eats any of these, call your vet, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at (888) 426-4435, or the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 — don't wait for symptoms. Below are the specifics for each.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Why is xylitol so dangerous for dogs?
answer: Xylitol is arguably the most dangerous common food toxin for dogs because it's potent and hidden in everyday products — sugar-free gum, mints, many peanut butters, baked goods, and some 'keto'/low-sugar foods. In dogs it triggers a massive insulin release: hypoglycemia (dangerously low blood sugar) can occur at roughly 0.1 g per kg of body weight, and liver failure at around 0.5 g/kg. A single piece of some sugar-free gum can contain enough to harm a small dog. Always check peanut butter labels before using it — this is a genuine emergency, so call your vet or poison control immediately.

question: How much chocolate is toxic to a dog?
answer: It depends on the type of chocolate and the dog's weight, because the toxic agent is theobromine (plus caffeine). The darker the chocolate, the more theobromine: baker's and dark chocolate are far more dangerous than milk chocolate, and white chocolate has almost none. As a rough guide, signs start around 20 mg of theobromine per kg of body weight, serious cardiac effects around 40–50 mg/kg, and seizures around 60 mg/kg. Practically, a few M&Ms won't hurt a large dog, but a bar of dark chocolate can seriously harm a small one. Symptoms (vomiting, restlessness, racing heart, tremors) can take 6–12 hours — call poison control with the type and amount eaten.

question: Are grapes and raisins really toxic to dogs, even a few?
answer: Yes — grapes, raisins, currants, and even foods containing them can cause acute kidney failure, and the reaction is unpredictable. Recent research points to tartaric acid as the likely toxic component, which dogs handle poorly. There is no established 'safe' amount: some dogs eat several with no effect while others have severe reactions to just a few, so all ingestion is treated as a potential emergency. Raisins are more concentrated than grapes and considered higher-risk. If your dog eats any, contact your vet or poison control right away — early treatment is key.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Are onions toxic to dogs?
answer: Yes. Onions (along with leeks, shallots, and chives) are in the allium family and contain compounds (organosulfur thiosulfates) that damage red blood cells and cause Heinz-body hemolytic anemia. Toxic effects in dogs are generally seen around 5 grams of onion per kg of body weight, and importantly the effect is cumulative — small amounts over time, or a single larger dose, can both cause it. All forms count, and cooked or powdered onion (common in broths, baby food, and seasonings) is just as dangerous, often more concentrated. Signs (weakness, pale gums, dark urine, lethargy) can be delayed several days.

question: Is garlic safe or toxic for dogs? (the honest answer)
answer: The truthful answer is: it's dose-dependent. Garlic is in the same allium family as onions and contains the same red-blood-cell-damaging thiosulfates, and at high doses it can cause Heinz-body hemolytic anemia — it's roughly 5x more concentrated than onion, so it takes less. The toxic studies that scared everyone used very large amounts (around 5 g/kg). However, the small amounts used in holistic practice — about 1/4 of a fresh clove per 10 lb of body weight — sit far below those toxic thresholds, which is why many holistic vets consider garlic safe and beneficial in moderation. Two firm rules: never give large or concentrated amounts, and never give garlic to CATS (they're far more sensitive and it can cause anemia). When in doubt, dose conservatively and ask a holistic vet.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Can dogs eat macadamia nuts?
answer: No — macadamia nuts are uniquely toxic to dogs, though the exact mechanism is unknown. Signs can appear at doses as low as about 2 grams per kg of body weight and include weakness (especially in the hind legs), tremors, vomiting, depression, and hyperthermia (elevated temperature). It's rarely fatal and dogs usually recover within 24–48 hours, but it's distressing and warrants a call to your vet. Watch out for them in cookies and trail mix. Most other nuts aren't 'toxic' but are high-fat (pancreatitis risk) and a choking/obstruction hazard.

question: Why are alcohol and raw bread dough dangerous for dogs?
answer: Both come down to ethanol. Alcohol (in drinks, but also some desserts and rotting fruit) causes dangerous drops in blood sugar, body temperature, and blood pressure, and can lead to seizures or respiratory failure — dogs are far more sensitive than people. Raw yeast bread dough is a double threat: the warm stomach makes it keep rising (causing painful bloat and possible stomach twisting), and the fermenting yeast produces alcohol that's absorbed into the bloodstream. Both are emergencies — call your vet or poison control.

question: Can dogs have caffeine or coffee?
answer: No. Caffeine (in coffee, tea, energy drinks, and even coffee grounds or beans) is a stimulant in the same chemical family as chocolate's theobromine, and dogs are very sensitive to it. It can cause restlessness, a racing heart, high blood pressure, tremors, and seizures. A few licks of brewed coffee likely won't harm a large dog, but coffee grounds, beans, or pills are concentrated and dangerous. Keep all caffeine sources out of reach and call poison control if your dog gets into them.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Can dogs eat avocado?
answer: Mostly yes, with caveats — this one is often overstated. Avocado contains persin, which is highly toxic to birds and some livestock, but dogs are fairly resistant and the flesh in small amounts is generally fine (it's even in some dog foods). The real hazards for dogs are the large pit (a serious choking and intestinal-obstruction risk) and the high fat content, which can trigger stomach upset or pancreatitis in sensitive dogs. So: a little plain avocado flesh is okay for most dogs, but skip the pit and skin and don't make it a fatty habit.

question: Are cooked bones or corn cobs dangerous for dogs?
answer: Yes, but as physical hazards rather than poisons. Cooked bones become brittle and splinter into sharp fragments that can damage or puncture the mouth, throat, and digestive tract — never feed cooked bones (raw meaty bones are a different, supervised discussion). Corn cobs are a classic cause of intestinal blockage because dogs swallow chunks that don't break down and lodge in the gut, often requiring surgery. Also watch fruit pits and large seeds. These won't poison your dog, but they cause real emergencies, so keep them out of reach.

question: What healthy human foods CAN dogs eat?
answer: Plenty of whole foods make excellent, healthy additions — this is the fun part of feeding holistically. Great options include blueberries, carrots, plain cooked pumpkin, eggs, plain yogurt or kefir, sardines, apple slices (no seeds), green beans, plain cooked sweet potato, watermelon (no seeds or rind), cucumber, and xylitol-free peanut butter. These add real nutrients, antioxidants, fiber, and omega-3s. The general rule: keep additions to about 10% of daily calories, introduce one new thing at a time, and serve them plain (no salt, sugar, butter, onion, or garlic seasoning).

question: Can dogs eat blueberries?
answer: Yes — blueberries are one of the best treats you can give. They're low in sugar and calories and packed with antioxidants (anthocyanins), vitamin C, and fiber that support the immune system and fight inflammation, which fits a holistic anti-inflammatory approach perfectly. Serve them fresh or frozen (frozen makes a great crunchy hot-weather treat). Just keep the quantity reasonable as part of the ~10% treat allowance. A genuinely healthy, dog-safe superfood.

question: Can dogs eat eggs?
answer: Yes — eggs are a fantastic whole-food protein for dogs, rich in highly digestible amino acids, plus biotin, riboflavin, and selenium. Cooked (plain, no butter or salt) is the safe default; some raw-feeders give raw eggs, which is generally fine from a clean source though it carries a small salmonella consideration and raw egg whites in large amounts can affect biotin. The shell, ground, even adds calcium. An egg a few times a week is a great topper for most dogs — scale the amount to your dog's size.

question: Can dogs eat pumpkin?
answer: Yes — plain cooked pumpkin (not pie filling, which has sugar and spices) is a holistic staple. Its soluble fiber helps with both diarrhea and constipation, it's gentle on the stomach, and it provides beta-carotene and potassium. A common amount is roughly a teaspoon to a tablespoon per meal depending on the dog's size. It's also a good carrier for supplements. Canned 100% pumpkin or fresh-cooked both work — just make sure there are no added sweeteners.

question: Can dogs have peanut butter?
answer: Yes — BUT you must check the label for xylitol first, because some peanut butters use that sweetener and it can be deadly to dogs. Choose a plain peanut butter whose only ingredient is peanuts (no added sugar, salt, or sweeteners). In moderation it's a useful high-value treat and a great way to give pills or stuff a frozen enrichment toy. Keep portions small since it's calorie- and fat-dense. Bottom line: xylitol-free, unsalted, and used as an occasional treat.

question: Can dogs eat dairy like milk, cheese, and yogurt?
answer: It depends on the dog and the type. Many adult dogs are somewhat lactose intolerant, so milk and heavy cheese can cause gas, loose stools, or upset. However, plain unsweetened yogurt and kefir are usually well tolerated and even beneficial, because fermentation reduces lactose and adds gut-friendly probiotics — a nice holistic addition for gut health. Avoid sweetened or flavored versions (watch for xylitol), and go easy on fatty cheeses, especially in dogs prone to pancreatitis. Start with a small amount to see how your dog handles it.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Are fatty or salty foods bad for dogs?
answer: Yes, in their own way — they're not 'toxic' like xylitol, but they cause real problems. High-fat foods (bacon, fried foods, fatty trimmings, lots of cheese) can trigger pancreatitis, a painful and sometimes serious inflammation of the pancreas, especially in prone breeds and overweight dogs. Very salty foods (chips, processed meats, large amounts of table scraps) can cause excessive thirst and, in extreme cases, sodium ion poisoning. Rich, fatty 'treats' are also a leading cause of holiday vet visits. Keep additions whole, plain, and moderate.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: What should I do if my dog ate something toxic?
answer: Act fast and don't wait for symptoms, since many toxins (grapes, onions, xylitol) cause delayed damage. Note what was eaten, roughly how much, and when, then call your veterinarian, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center at (888) 426-4435, or the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 — they can tell you if it's an emergency. Do NOT induce vomiting unless a professional tells you to, because for some substances it makes things worse. For fast-acting, dangerous items (xylitol, chocolate, grapes, alcohol), getting help in the first hour or two makes a big difference.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack

question: Can dogs eat apples, carrots, and other common fruits and veggies?
answer: Yes — most are great, with a couple of simple rules. Safe and healthy choices include apples (remove the core and seeds — apple seeds contain trace cyanide compounds, harmless in small amounts but best avoided), carrots (a crunchy low-calorie favorite, good for teeth), green beans, cucumber, celery, watermelon (no seeds or rind), banana (small amounts, higher sugar), and berries. Stick to plain, washed, appropriately sized pieces, avoid the toxic ones (grapes/raisins, onions/garlic in quantity), and remember pits and large seeds are choking/obstruction hazards. Variety of dog-safe produce adds fiber, antioxidants, and enrichment.
source: Common Sense Dog — Toxic & Safe Foods pack
